why: Enclose and subtract: 6 × 4 = 24, then subtract the missing 2 × 2 = 4. 24 − 4 = 20 square units.
tip: Find the area of the whole rectangle, then subtract what is missing.

opts: To subtract the parts of the rectangle that are not part of the shape.
To add the parts that are not shaded.
why: Enclosing is only the first step; the unshaded corners inside the rectangle must be subtracted.
tip: Enclose AND subtract — both steps are needed.

q: An 8-by-3 rectangle has a 3-by-3 square attached to the top of it. What is the total area?
why: 8 × 3 = 24 and 3 × 3 = 9. 24 + 9 = 33 square units.
tip: Decompose into two rectangles and add.

opts: They must have the same perimeter.
They cover the same amount of space, even if their shapes are different.
why: Area only measures the space covered. Many different shapes can have the same area.
tip: Same area does not mean same shape or same perimeter.

A triangle with two equal sides
Any shape with four right angles only
A quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides
why: A parallelogram is a four-sided polygon whose opposite sides are parallel.
tip: Para-llel-ogram: both pairs of opposite sides are parallel.

q: Is a rectangle a parallelogram?
opts: Yes — both pairs of its opposite sides are parallel.
Only if it is a square.
No — a rectangle has right angles.
why: A rectangle has two pairs of parallel opposite sides, so it is a special kind of parallelogram.
tip: Check the definition, not just how the shape looks.

q: A triangle is cut off one side of a parallelogram and moved to the other side to make a rectangle. Why does this help find the area?
opts: The rectangle has the same base, height, and area as the parallelogram.
It changes the base into the slanted side.
The rectangle is bigger, so it is easier to count.
why: No area is added or lost when the piece moves, and the rectangle keeps the same base and height. So area = base × height.
tip: Decompose and rearrange keeps area the same.

q: What is true about the opposite sides of every parallelogram?
opts: They are parallel and the same length.
why: In a parallelogram, each pair of opposite sides is parallel and equal in length.
tip: Opposite sides match in a parallelogram.

q: Parallelogram A has base 5 and height 4. Parallelogram B has base 5 and height 4 but leans much farther. How do their areas compare?
opts: You cannot tell without the slanted sides.
A is larger because it is more upright.
B is larger because it leans more.
why: Area of a parallelogram depends only on base and height: 5 × 4 = 20 for both.
tip: The lean (slant) does not change the area if base and height stay the same.

q: A parallelogram has a base of 6 units, slanted sides of 5 units, and a height of 4 units. What is its area?
why: Use base × height: 6 × 4 = 24. The slanted side (5) is not the height.
tip: Height must be perpendicular to the base — ignore the slanted side.

opts: A trapezoid with only one pair of parallel sides
why: Squares, rhombuses and rectangles all have two pairs of parallel sides. A trapezoid like this has only one pair.
tip: Look for TWO pairs of parallel sides.

q: A parallelogram on a grid has a base of 7 units and a height of 2 units. What is its area?
why: 7 × 2 = 14 square units.
tip: Area of a parallelogram = base × height.

q: A parallelogram has a base of 8 units and a height of 2.5 units. What is its area?
why: 8 × 2.5 = 20 square units.
tip: Multiply base by height even when one is a decimal.

q: Which is the most precise description of a parallelogram?
opts: A shape that looks pushed over
A four-sided polygon with both pairs of opposite sides parallel
A polygon with four equal sides
why: Precise math language uses the defining property: four sides, both pairs of opposite sides parallel.
tip: Describe shapes by their properties, not how they look.

q: A parallelogram has a base of 9 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is its area?
why: 9 × 4 = 36 square centimeters.
tip: Area of a parallelogram = base × height.

q: A parallelogram has an area of 40 in² and a base of 10 in. What is its height?
why: Base × height = area, so 10 × ? = 40. The height is 4 inches.
tip: Divide the area by the base to find the height.

tip: Height makes a right angle with the base.

q: A parallelogram has an area of 54 square feet and a height of 6 feet. What is the base?
why: Base × 6 = 54, so the base is 54 ÷ 6 = 9 feet.
tip: Missing side = area ÷ the side you know.

q: Which statement about base and height is true?
opts: The height is always the slanted side.
Any side can be the base, and the height must be perpendicular to that base.
Only the bottom side can be the base.
The height must be inside the shape and touch a vertex at the center.
why: Any side can be chosen as the base. Its height is the perpendicular distance from that base to the opposite side.
tip: Choose a base, then find its matching perpendicular height.

q: A parallelogram has a base of 7.5 m and a height of 4 m. What is its area?
tip: Multiply base by height.

q: A parallelogram has an area of 63 square units and a base of 9 units. What is its height?
why: 63 ÷ 9 = 7 units.
tip: Divide area by base.

q: A rectangle and a parallelogram both have a base of 6 cm and a height of 4 cm. Which is true?
opts: The rectangle has a bigger area.
The parallelogram has an area of 12 cm².
The parallelogram has a bigger area.
They both have an area of 24 cm².
why: Both use base × height: 6 × 4 = 24 cm².
tip: A parallelogram can be rearranged into a rectangle with the same base and height.

q: Parallelogram A has base 8 and height 3. Parallelogram B has base 6 and height 5. Which is larger, and by how much?
why: A = 8 × 3 = 24. B = 6 × 5 = 30. 30 − 24 = 6, so B is larger by 6 square units.
tip: Find both areas, then compare.

q: A parallelogram has a base of 2.5 m and a height of 1.2 m. What is its area?
tip: Decimal multiplication: 25 × 12 = 300, then place the decimal.

q: Which base and height could belong to a parallelogram with an area of 36 square inches?
why: 9 × 4 = 36. The others multiply to 243, 180 and 288.
tip: The base times the height must equal the area.

q: A parallelogram has a base of 12 units and a height of 3 units. If the base is doubled and the height stays the same, what is the new area?
why: Original area: 12 × 3 = 36. New base 24: 24 × 3 = 72, which is double the area.
tip: Doubling one dimension doubles the area.

q: A parallelogram has an area of 45 cm² and a height of 7.5 cm. What is the length of the base?
tip: Divide the area by the height to get the base.

q: A parallelogram has sides of 10 cm and 6 cm. The height to the 10 cm base is 5 cm. What is the height to the 6 cm base (to the nearest hundredth)?
why: Area = 10 × 5 = 50 cm². Using the 6 cm side as the base: 6 × h = 50, so h = 50 ÷ 6 ≈ 8.33 cm.
tip: The area is the same no matter which base you use.

q: A wall section is shaped like a parallelogram with a base of 15 ft and a height of 8 ft. One can of paint covers 40 square feet. How many cans are needed?
tip: Find the area first, then divide by the coverage of one can.

q: Two identical triangles are put together along one side. What shape can they make?
opts: A trapezoid with one parallel pair only
why: Two copies of any triangle can be arranged into a parallelogram. That is why a triangle's area is half of a parallelogram's.
tip: Two copies of a triangle = one parallelogram.

q: A square with a side of 6 units is cut along a diagonal. What is the area of each triangle?
why: The square has area 36. The diagonal cuts it into two equal triangles, so each is 36 ÷ 2 = 18 square units.
tip: A diagonal splits a square into two equal halves.

q: A parallelogram with an area of 30 square units is cut along a diagonal. What is the area of each triangle?
why: A diagonal cuts a parallelogram into two identical triangles. 30 ÷ 2 = 15 square units each.
tip: Each triangle is half of the parallelogram.

q: A student counted only the 6 whole squares inside a triangle and said its area is 6 square units. What mistake did they make?
opts: They ignored the partial squares that are also inside the triangle.
They should have counted the grid lines.
why: Partial squares also cover part of the triangle and must be counted (for example, two halves make one whole).
tip: Count whole squares AND combine the partial ones.

q: A triangle on a grid has a base of 5 units and a height of 5 units. What is its area?
tip: Area can be a decimal when you halve an odd number.

q: Which two triangles must have the same area?
opts: Two triangles with one equal side
Two triangles with the same base length and the same height
Two triangles that both have a right angle
Two triangles with the same perimeter
why: Area of a triangle depends only on base and height, so equal bases and equal heights mean equal areas.
tip: Base and height decide the area.

q: A triangle on a grid has a base of 10 units and a height of 3 units. What is its area?
why: (10 × 3) ÷ 2 = 15 square units.
tip: Multiply, then halve.

q: Why does the area of a triangle equal (base × height) ÷ 2?
opts: Because triangles have 3 sides and rectangles have 4.
Two copies of the triangle make a parallelogram with the same base and height, and the triangle is half of it.
Because you always divide area by 2.
Because the height is half the base.
why: Any triangle and a copy of it form a parallelogram (area = base × height). The triangle is one half of that.
tip: Connect triangles back to parallelograms.

q: A right triangle on a grid has legs of 7 units and 4 units. What is its area?
why: (7 × 4) ÷ 2 = 14 square units.
tip: In a right triangle, the two legs are a base and its height.

q: Two triangles have the same base of 6 units. Triangle A has a height of 4 units and Triangle B has a height of 8 units. Which statement is true?
opts: B's area is twice A's area.
A's area is twice B's area.
B's area is 4 square units more.
tip: Doubling the height doubles the area.

She should have added; the area is 11 square units.

why: Base × height gives the parallelogram's area. The triangle is half: 28 ÷ 2 = 14 square units.
tip: Always halve for a triangle.

q: The height of a triangle can be drawn outside the triangle. When does this happen?
opts: Only when the triangle is a right triangle
When the triangle has an obtuse angle at one end of the base
Never — the height is always inside
Only when all sides are equal
why: In an obtuse triangle, the perpendicular from the top vertex can land on the extension of the base, outside the triangle.
tip: Extend the base with a dashed line if needed.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.6 (Generalizing the Area of a Triangle)
q: Triangle A has base 6 and height 8. Triangle B has base 8 and height 6. Which statement is true?
opts: They each have area 48 square units.
They have the same area, 24 square units.
why: ½ × 6 × 8 = 24 and ½ × 8 × 6 = 24. Swapping base and height does not change the product.
tip: Order does not matter when multiplying.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.6 (Generalizing the Area of a Triangle)
q: A triangle has a base of 3.5 m and a height of 4 m. What is its area?
tip: Multiply first, then halve.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.6 (Generalizing the Area of a Triangle)
q: A right triangle has sides of 9 cm, 12 cm and 15 cm. What is its area?
why: In a right triangle the two shorter sides (legs) are perpendicular, so use them as base and height: ½ × 9 × 12 = 54 cm². The 15 cm side is the slanted hypotenuse.
tip: Use the two sides that meet at the right angle.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.6 (Generalizing the Area of a Triangle)
q: A triangle has an area of 20 square units. If both its base and its height are doubled, what is the new area?
why: Doubling the base doubles the area (40), and doubling the height doubles it again: 80 square units.
tip: Doubling both dimensions multiplies area by 4.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.6 (Generalizing the Area of a Triangle)
q: Han says a triangle with base 10 and height 6 has the same area as a parallelogram with base 5 and height 6. Is he correct?
opts: No — the triangle has 60 square units.
Yes — both have an area of 30 square units.
No — triangles always have less area than parallelograms.
No — the parallelogram has 15 square units.
why: Triangle: ½ × 10 × 6 = 30. Parallelogram: 5 × 6 = 30. They are equal.
tip: Compute each area before comparing shapes.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: A triangle has a base of 14 ft and a height of 6 ft. What is its area?
tip: A = ½ × b × h.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: Triangles A and B have the same base, but Triangle A is taller. Which has the greater area?
why: Area depends on base and height. The bases are equal, and A has the greater height, so A has the greater area.
tip: Same base: the taller triangle has more area.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: Aki found a triangle's area using the base and a slanted side instead of the height. What should Aki do?
opts: Nothing — any side can be the height.
Use a height that is perpendicular to the base Aki chose.
Use the longest side as the height.
Add the base and the slanted side.
why: The height must make a right angle with the base. A slanted side is not a height.
tip: Base and height must be perpendicular.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: A right triangle has legs of 5 m and 8 m. What is its area?
tip: The legs of a right triangle are a base and its height.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: A triangular sail has a base of 6 ft and a height of 9 ft. How much fabric is needed?
why: ½ × 6 × 9 = 27 square feet.
tip: Fabric covers area, so use the area formula.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: A triangle has an area of 24 cm². Which base and height could it have?
why: For area 24, base × height must be 48. 8 × 6 = 48, so ½ × 48 = 24 cm².
tip: Base × height should equal double the area.

q: Which measurement is NOT needed to find the area of a triangle?
opts: The length of a slanted side that is not the base
A base and its matching height
why: Only a base and its perpendicular height are needed. Other side lengths are extra information.
tip: Spot and ignore extra measurements.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: A triangle has an area of 45 in² and a height of 9 in. What is the base?
tip: Double the area, then divide by the height.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: A triangle has a base of 7 cm and a height of 7 cm. What is its area?
tip: Halving an odd product gives a .5 decimal.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: A rectangle is 12 by 8 (area 96). Two right triangles with areas 48 and 12 are cut away, leaving one triangle. What is the area of that triangle?
why: 96 − 48 − 12 = 36 square units.
tip: Enclose and subtract works off the grid too.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: A triangle has an area of 30 m². Using one side of 12 m as the base, the height is 5 m. What is the height if a side of 10 m is used as the base instead?
why: The area is still 30 m². ½ × 10 × h = 30 → 5h = 30 → h = 6 m.
tip: A triangle has three base-height pairs, all giving the same area.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: An isosceles triangle has sides of 13 cm, 13 cm and 10 cm. The height to the 10 cm side is 12 cm. What is its area?
why: Use the 10 cm base and its 12 cm height: ½ × 10 × 12 = 60 cm². The 13 cm sides are not heights.
tip: Pick the base that has a known perpendicular height.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: A triangular garden has a base of 20 m and a height of 15 m. One bag of fertilizer covers 50 m². How many bags are needed?
tip: Find the area, then divide by the coverage of one bag.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.7 (Applying the Triangle Area Formula)
q: A kite is made of two triangles that share a 10-inch base. Each triangle has a height of 3 inches. What is the area of the kite?
why: Each triangle: ½ × 10 × 3 = 15 in². Two triangles: 15 + 15 = 30 in².
tip: Decompose the shape into triangles and add.

q: Which describes a polygon?
opts: A closed shape made of straight sides that do not cross
An open shape made of line segments
why: Polygons are closed, have only straight sides, and the sides never cross.
tip: No curves, no gaps, no crossings.

q: Why is a circle NOT a polygon?
why: Polygons only have straight sides. A circle is curved.
tip: Polygons have straight sides only.

q: What is the area of the polygon?
img: <svg viewBox="0 0 276 270" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="width:100%;max-width:276px"><polygon points="44,16 180,118 180,186 44,186" fill="#EEF1F8" fill-opacity="0.85" stroke="#2B3242" stroke-width="3" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="44" y1="16" x2="180" y2="16" stroke="#4F46E5" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6,5"/><line x1="180" y1="16" x2="180" y2="118" stroke="#4F46E5" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="6,5"/><text x="112" y="218" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#2B3242" text-anchor="middle">4 in</text><text x="24" y="109" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#2B3242" text-anchor="middle">5 in</text><text x="204" y="75" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#2B3242" text-anchor="middle">3 in</text></svg>
why: Draw a 4 in by 5 in rectangle around it (20 in²) and subtract the missing triangle: (4 × 3) ÷ 2 = 6 in². 20 − 6 = 14 in².
tip: Enclose with a rectangle and subtract the missing triangle.

q: A polygon is made of a rectangle that is 8 cm by 6 cm with a triangle on top that has a base of 8 cm and a height of 3 cm. What is its area?
why: Rectangle: 8 × 6 = 48 cm². Triangle: (8 × 3) ÷ 2 = 12 cm². 48 + 12 = 60 cm².
tip: Decompose into shapes you know and add their areas.

q: Kai found the area of a polygon by decomposing it. Lena found it by enclosing it and subtracting. If both are done correctly, what is true?
opts: Only one method works for polygons.
why: Area is a fixed amount. Any correct strategy gives the same answer.
tip: Different strategies, same area.

q: A house-shaped pentagon has a rectangle 6 units wide and 4 units tall, with a triangular roof 3 units tall on top. What is its area?
why: Rectangle: 6 × 4 = 24. Roof: (6 × 3) ÷ 2 = 9. 24 + 9 = 33 square units.
tip: Split the pentagon into a rectangle and a triangle.

q: An L-shaped polygon fits in an 8 by 6 rectangle, with a 5 by 4 rectangle missing from one corner. What is its area?
why: Enclose and subtract: 8 × 6 = 48, minus 5 × 4 = 20. 48 − 20 = 28 square units.
tip: Subtract the missing rectangle from the whole rectangle.

q: Callen found the area of a quadrilateral by using the formula for a parallelogram. Its opposite sides are not parallel. What is wrong?
opts: The shape is not a parallelogram, so base × height does not apply; he should decompose it.
He should have added the sides.
Nothing — every quadrilateral is a parallelogram.
why: The parallelogram formula only works when both pairs of opposite sides are parallel. Otherwise, break the shape into rectangles and triangles.
tip: Check the shape's properties before choosing a formula.

q: What is the area of the polygon?

why: Middle rectangle: 10 × 4 = 40. Each side triangle has base 4 and height 3: (4 × 3) ÷ 2 = 6, and there are 2. 40 + 12 = 52 square units.
tip: Decompose into one rectangle and two triangles.

q: An arrow is made of a rectangle 6 by 2 and a triangle with a base of 4 and a height of 3. What is its area?
why: Rectangle: 6 × 2 = 12. Triangle: (4 × 3) ÷ 2 = 6. 12 + 6 = 18 square units.
tip: Add the area of each piece.

q: A trapezoid has parallel sides of 6 cm and 10 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is its area?
why: Decompose into a 6 × 4 rectangle (24) and triangles with total base 4 and height 4 ((4 × 4) ÷ 2 = 8). 24 + 8 = 32 cm².
tip: A trapezoid can be split into a rectangle and triangles.

q: A trapezoid has parallel sides of 5 m and 9 m and a height of 6 m. What is its area?
why: Two copies make a parallelogram with base 5 + 9 = 14 and height 6 (area 84). One trapezoid is half: 42 m².
tip: Two identical trapezoids make a parallelogram.

q: A polygon fits inside a 5 by 6 rectangle with one right triangle (legs 5 and 2) missing. What is the area of the polygon?
why: Rectangle: 5 × 6 = 30. Missing triangle: (5 × 2) ÷ 2 = 5. 30 − 5 = 25 square units.
tip: Enclose, then subtract.

q: An octagon is made by cutting four corner triangles off a 9 cm by 9 cm square. Each corner triangle is a right triangle with legs of 3 cm. What is the octagon's area?
tip: Subtract all four corners.

q: A polygon is made of a 12 m by 5 m rectangle with a triangle (base 12 m, height 4 m) on top and a 3 m by 3 m square cut out of the rectangle. What is its area?
why: Rectangle 60 + triangle (12 × 4) ÷ 2 = 24 → 84. Subtract the 9 m² square: 84 − 9 = 75 m².
tip: Add the pieces that are there, subtract the piece that is missing.

q: How is a pyramid different from a prism?
opts: A pyramid has no flat faces.
A pyramid has two bases; a prism has one.
A pyramid has one base and triangular faces that meet at a point; a prism has two identical bases.
why: A prism has two identical, parallel bases joined by rectangles. A pyramid has one base and triangles that meet at a vertex.
tip: Prism = 2 bases. Pyramid = 1 base + a point.

q: How many faces does a triangular prism have?
why: 2 triangular bases + 3 rectangular faces = 5 faces.
tip: Count the bases and the faces connecting them.

q: Which is NOT a polyhedron?
why: A cylinder has curved surfaces. Polyhedra have only flat polygon faces.
tip: Polyhedra: flat faces only.

q: How many faces does a square pyramid have?
why: 1 square base + 4 triangles = 5 faces.
tip: Pyramid faces = base + one triangle per side of the base.

q: What is a net?
opts: A flat, 2-D figure that can be folded into a 3-D shape
why: A net is the shape you get by unfolding a polyhedron so all its faces lie flat.
tip: Think of a cereal box cut open and laid flat.

q: A net has 2 triangles and 3 rectangles. What polyhedron does it make?
why: Two triangular bases joined by three rectangles form a triangular prism.
tip: Two matching bases + rectangles → prism.

q: A net has 1 square and 4 triangles. What polyhedron does it make?
why: One square base with four triangles meeting at a point is a square pyramid.
tip: One base + triangles → pyramid.

q: Kira's prism has 10 faces. What shape are its bases?
why: Every prism has 2 bases, so there are 10 − 2 = 8 rectangular faces. Each base must have 8 sides — an octagon.
tip: Prism faces = sides of the base + 2.

q: How many faces does a hexagonal pyramid have?
why: 1 hexagon base + 6 triangles = 7 faces.
tip: Pyramid faces = number of base sides + 1.

q: A pyramid has 6 faces in all. What shape is its base?
why: 6 − 1 base = 5 triangles, so the base has 5 sides: a pentagon.
tip: Subtract the base to count the triangles.

q: Which statement about a triangular pyramid is true?
opts: All 4 of its faces are triangles.
why: A triangular pyramid has a triangular base and 3 triangular sides, so 4 triangle faces.
tip: The base of a triangular pyramid is also a triangle.

q: A prism has 7 faces. What shape is its base?
why: 7 − 2 bases = 5 rectangular faces, so the base has 5 sides.
tip: Prism: faces − 2 = sides of the base.

q: How many edges does a pentagonal prism have?
why: Each pentagon base has 5 edges (10 total) and there are 5 edges connecting the bases. 10 + 5 = 15.
tip: Prism edges = 3 × number of base sides.

q: How can you tell from a net that it folds into a prism?
opts: It has two identical faces (the bases) connected by rectangles.
All of its faces are triangles.
It has one face and all the rest are triangles.
why: Prisms have two identical bases joined by rectangles; pyramids have one base and triangles.
tip: Look for two matching bases.

q: A hexagonal prism has how many faces, edges, and vertices?
why: Faces: 2 hexagons + 6 rectangles = 8. Edges: 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. Vertices: 6 on each base = 12.
tip: Count each base separately, then the parts connecting them.

The total area of all the faces of a 3-D shape
The area of only the base

q: A cube has edges of 3 units. What is its surface area?
why: Each face: 3 × 3 = 9. Six faces: 6 × 9 = 54 square units.
tip: Surface area of a cube = 6 × (edge × edge).

q: Which arrangement of 6 squares will NOT fold into a cube?
opts: A cross shape (4 in a column with 1 on each side)
A "T" shape of 4 in a row with one above and one below the second square
All 6 squares in one straight row
A row of 4 with one square above the first and one below the last
why: Six squares in a row would wrap around and overlap, leaving two open ends. The other arrangements fold into a closed cube.
tip: Imagine folding — do any faces overlap or leave a gap?

q: How many faces are in the net of a triangular prism?
why: 2 triangles + 3 rectangles = 5 faces.
tip: A net shows every face exactly once.

q: A rectangular prism measures 2 by 3 by 4 units. What is its surface area?
why: Faces come in pairs: 2 × (2 × 3) + 2 × (2 × 4) + 2 × (3 × 4) = 12 + 16 + 24 = 52 square units.
tip: A rectangular prism has 3 pairs of identical faces.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.10 (Nets and Surface Area on a Grid)
q: A square pyramid has a 4-by-4 base. Each triangular face has a base of 4 and a height of 3. What is its surface area?
why: Base: 4 × 4 = 16. Each triangle: (4 × 3) ÷ 2 = 6, and there are 4: 24. 16 + 24 = 40 square units.
tip: Add the base and all the triangles.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.10 (Nets and Surface Area on a Grid)
q: Which rectangular prism has a surface area of 22 square units?
tip: Use 2 × (lw + lh + wh).

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.10 (Nets and Surface Area on a Grid)
q: A 1-by-1-by-5 prism and a 1-by-2-by-3 prism have the same surface area (22 square units). What about their volumes?
opts: They are different: 5 and 6 cubic units.
why: Volume = l × w × h: 1 × 1 × 5 = 5 and 1 × 2 × 3 = 6. Same surface area does not mean same volume.
tip: Surface area and volume measure different things.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.10 (Nets and Surface Area on a Grid)
q: A 1-by-2-by-2 prism has a volume of 4 cubic units. A 1-by-1-by-4 prism has the same volume. What are their surface areas?
tip: Same volume can have different surface areas.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.10 (Nets and Surface Area on a Grid)
q: A rectangular prism measures 2 by 2 by 5 units. What is its surface area?
why: Two 2 × 2 ends (8) and four 2 × 5 sides (40). 8 + 40 = 48 square units.
tip: Group identical faces to speed up the work.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.10 (Nets and Surface Area on a Grid)
q: A triangular prism has right-triangle bases with sides 3, 4 and 5 and is 6 units long. What is its surface area?
why: Two triangles: 2 × (3 × 4) ÷ 2 = 12. Three rectangles: 3 × 6 + 4 × 6 + 5 × 6 = 72. 12 + 72 = 84 square units.
tip: The rectangles' widths match the triangle's three sides.

source: slides:Acc6 Lesson 1.10 (Nets and Surface Area on a Grid)
q: Prism A has faces with areas 60, 80, 100, 24 and 24. Prism B has four faces of 60 and two faces of 36. Which has the greater surface area, and by how much?
tip: Add every face for each prism, then compare.

q: A cube has a surface area of 96 square inches. What is the length of each edge?
why: 96 ÷ 6 = 16 square inches per face, and 4 × 4 = 16, so each edge is 4 in.
tip: Divide by 6 to get one face, then find the side.

q: If every edge of a cube is doubled, what happens to its surface area?
why: Each face goes from s × s to 2s × 2s = 4 × s². All 6 faces grow by 4 times, so the surface area is 4 times as large.
tip: Area grows by the scale factor squared.
